prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a focal neurological sign (right-sided motor asymmetry) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of the focal neurological sign (right-sided motor asymmetry) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Resuscitate sepsis with hypotension (90/54 mmHg) and blood lactate 4.1 mmol/L: IV crystalloid (about 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours), vasopressors to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg if hypotension persists, and repeat lactate (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021). Repeat platelets, fibrinogen, INR and D-dimer: the low fibrinogen (179 mg/dL) with raised D-dimer, INR 1.3 and platelets 147 indicate a sepsis-associated coagulopathy that may progress to DIC.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L is susceptible by CLSI meningitis breakpoints, so benzylpenicillin or continued ceftriaxone for Streptococcus pneumoniae; stop ampicillin.
ENT assessment for drainage of the maxillary and ethmoid sinus source.

Obtain contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain if the right-sided motor asymmetry persists or she fails to improve, to look for subdural empyema, cerebritis or venous sinus thrombosis from the sinus source.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).
Resuscitate the hypotension before the lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 A.1.1; NICE NG240 1.4.11); antibiotics and dexamethasone are not delayed for it.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of the focal neurological sign (right-sided motor asymmetry) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: focal neurological signs (less movement of the right limbs than the left in an obtunded patient). NICE NG240 1.4.7 agrees (new focal neurological features). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

patient.history_present_illness: This 38-year-old right-handed woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and recurrent sinusitis was brought to the emergency department by her wife after approximately 10 hours of rapidly progressive symptoms. According to her wife, the patient had been experiencing worsening frontal headaches and purulent nasal discharge for the previous four days, which they attributed to another flare of her chronic sinusitis. She had been self-treating with over-the-counter nasal decongestants and ibuprofen. Yesterday evening, she developed rigors, and her temperature at home was measured at 39.2 degrees Celsius. She took acetaminophen 1000 mg but the fever did not abate. By approximately midnight, her wife noticed she was becoming increasingly confused, calling her by the wrong name and unable to recall what day it was. She found her sitting in the dark bathroom complaining that the lights were too bright and that a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache was radiating down the back of her neck. She attempted to get her to look down at her chest and she cried out in pain. By early morning, she had become progressively more lethargic and difficult to rouse, prompting the call to emergency services. Upon arrival by ambulance, the patient was febrile to 39.5 degrees Celsius with a heart rate of 116, blood pressure of 90/54, and was noted to be obtunded and minimally responsive to verbal commands. There had been no witnessed seizures, no vomiting, no rash, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts. She received a 1-liter normal saline bolus and was transferred to the resuscitation bay.
